title: Hanbury-Brown Twiss effect, squeezed gravitons and the photon correlations
abstract: Unlike the gravitational waves classically generated by moving macroscopic masses, the diffuse backgrounds of gravitons originate most likely from zero-point fluctuations of the gravitational field amplified by the evolution of the space-time curvature. The resulting entangled states lead to specific second-order correlation effects that could be eventually detected. For a quantitative analysis of this empirical expectation we scrutinize the interactions between the cosmic gravitons and the fundamental mode of a quantized electromagnetic field confined inside a closed optical resonator with perfectly-reflecting walls. We show that the Hanbury-Brown Twiss correlations of the photons are insensitive to the degrees of second-order coherence of the gravitons even barring for the exceedingly small couplings of the problem. Since the degree of second-order coherence of the photons does not reflect the correlation properties of the gravitons, the statistical properties of the gravitons (and their super-Poissonian statistics) cannot be inferred, even in principle, from the intensity correlations of the cavity modes.
summary: This paper investigates the possibility of measuring relic gravitational wave statistics using photon interference in an optical cavity. By analyzing the coupled action and coherence functions, the authors prove that due to underlying symmetries, the measured Hanbury-Brown Twiss correlations of the photons are completely insensitive to the statistical properties of the gravitons. This places a fundamental limit on what can be inferred about the early universe's gravitational background from current photon measurements.
main_problem: To determine if Hanbury-Brown Twiss (HBT) correlations measured from photons confined in an optical cavity can reveal the super-Poissonian statistical properties of relic gravitons interacting with them.
main_result: The HBT correlations of the cavity photons are insensitive to the second-order coherence of the gravitons, meaning the graviton statistics cannot be inferred from photon intensity measurements.
method: The analysis uses generalized Glauber correlators extended to tensor fields (for gravitons) and electromagnetic fields (for photons), analyzing the total action derived from coupling gravity and electromagnetism.
model_or_system: The system models the interaction between cosmic relic gravitons (from zero-point fluctuations) and a quantized electromagnetic field confined within a closed optical resonator. The Hamiltonian analysis shows that the cavity photon number operator commutes with the full Hamiltonian, leading to the decoupling of coherence measurements.
key_observables: Hanbury-Brown Twiss correlations ($g^{(2)}$), first-order coherence ($g^{(1)}$), and the degree of second-order coherence for both photons and gravitons.
important_parameters: Cosmic graviton wavenumbers $O(k_p)$ ($\approx 0.002 	ext{ Mpc}^{-1}$); tensor-to-scalar ratio ($r_T$); small coupling limits.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on extending Glauber correlators to tensor cases and assumes a conformally flat background metric for the action derivation.
figures_summary: Not specified in notes, but the structure implies derivations of correlators (Eq. 2.16) and Hamiltonian evolution equations (B.10-B.17).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing generalized Glauber correlators for vector/tensor fields, then applying these to derive the total action coupling photons and gravitons, culminating in a symmetry argument showing that photon coherence is decoupled from graviton statistics.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous theoretical framework demonstrating fundamental limitations on experimental detection methods by proving that certain quantum correlations (graviton statistics) cannot be accessed via simpler measurements (photon intensity correlation).

figures.caption: Figure 1: We illustrate the geometry of a cavity where the walls are located along the ˆx direction. If ˆk = ˆx the gravitational wave propagates long the cavity axis. In the other cases the gravitational wave propagates orthogonally to the axis of the cavity.
Figure 2: The common logarithm of the effective coupling is illustrated as a function of the frequen- cies of the gravitons and of the photons.

Figure 3: We approximately illustrate here the effective evolution of the comoving Hubble radius H as a function of the scale factor a. Common logarithms are employed on both axes. During the inflationary stage H ∝a while during the radiation and matter stages H ∝a−1 and H ∝a−1/2, respectively. What matters for the evolution of the field operators are the exit and reentry times corresponding to the moments where a given wavenumber crosses the comoving horizon. The reentry and the exit approximately coincide close to the maximal wavenumber of the spectrum kmax.
